descriptions.default: Nephthys and Isis kneel side by side, their name signs on their heads, at the end of the night journey.
Nut, the sky goddess, bends low over the earth. Beneath her lie a lion and a scarab: the sun, soon to be born again from her body.
Osiris sits on his throne in the tall atef crown, holding a sceptre. "My fair goal is with Osiris," says the dead man.
A tall stand with a loaf and a lotus flower, set before Osiris.
The dead man raises his hands in praise before Osiris.
Anubis, the jackal-headed god of embalming, stands behind the dead man as he worships Osiris.
A man carries a chest high on one hand. It may be the burial chest named near the end of the spell.
Nephthys and Isis raise a hand toward the boat; Isis holds an ankh. Isis destroys what is wrong in the dead man, and Nephthys cuts away what rebels.
Two baboons stand upright and raise their paws in praise of the evening sun.
Atum, the evening sun, crowned with the sun disc, sits in his boat before a stand with a lotus. Spell 17 opens in his voice: "I am Atum."
Two baboons stand upright and raise their paws in praise of the evening sun.
Isis and Nephthys stand with a hand raised, each holding an ankh. "I was conceived by Isis and begotten by Nephthys," says the dead man.
Two baboons squat on their haunches facing Khepri's boat, greeting the rising sun.
Khepri, the god with a scarab for a head, rides in the boat of the rising sun. "O Khepri in the midst of your boat," the dead man prays, "deliver me."
The running caption of Spell 17 above plate IX, with remnants of signs.
The dead man kneels with both hands raised before Khepri's boat.
Two baboons squat facing the scarab god's boat. In another copy such apes stand for Isis and Nephthys.
A falcon perches on a tall standard, a flail at its back. Perhaps it shows the words "I fly like a falcon."
"I am the great Cat by the Persea tree in Heliopolis." The cat is Ra himself, cutting off the head of the snake Apep, enemy of the sun.
The sacred persea tree of Heliopolis, where the great cat fights the snake.
A small figure sits beside the tree with one knee drawn up. Who it is is not known.
Two bearded gods sit on thrones: probably the pair in whom one soul dwells, Osiris and Ra, who meet in Djedu and embrace.
Two ribbed bowls stand side by side with signs heaped on them. What they show is not known.
A god stands beneath a pair of eyes: Horus Khenty-irty, "Horus foremost of the two eyes", one of the Seven Spirits.

spirit_with_emblem.name: Spirit with a sign on his head

descriptions.default: A bearded god with a curled sign on his head: one of the Seven Spirits who, with the sons of Horus, follow the coffin of Osiris. Which of the Seven he is could not be identified.
A mummy-shaped god with a jackal's head: Duamutef, one of the four sons of Horus who guard the burial.
A mummy-shaped god with a human head: Imsety, one of the four sons of Horus who guard the burial.
A head rises from the top of a tall burial chest guarded by the four sons of Horus: the sun god coming up out of the burial.
A mummy-shaped god with a baboon's head: Hapy, one of the four sons of Horus who guard the burial.
A mummy-shaped god with a falcon's head: Qebehsenuef, one of the four sons of Horus who guard the burial.
The great cow of the sky lies on a shrine, a flail on her back and a sun disc with plumes on her head. At her udders, the spell says, Ra is born again each day.
The running caption of Spell 17 above plate VIII, with remnants of signs.
A man holds up a small offering to the great cow. In another copy Thoth offers her the Eye of Horus.
The wedjat eye rests on a shrine: the Eye of Horus, made whole again after his battle with Seth.
A baboon squats facing the Eye of Horus. It is probably Thoth, who in the spell lifts the veil of darkness from the Eye.
A tall gate with a snake inside and three blades on its roof: the gate through which the sun god goes out to the eastern horizon.
Two gods kneel, each reaching a hand over a small pool: Heh, god of millions of years, and Wadj-wer, the Great Green. In the two lakes, of Natron and of Maat, the dead man is purified.
Nephthys in the form of a kite, her sign of a basket on a house on her head, mourns at the head of the bier.
The mummy lies on a bier shaped like a lion, mourned by Isis and Nephthys as kites at its foot and head.
Isis in the form of a kite, her throne sign on her head, mourns at the foot of the bier.
The Benu heron. "I am the great Heron who is in Heliopolis," says the dead man: Osiris, who keeps the account of all that is and all that will be.
The other lion of the horizon, named Tomorrow in other copies: Ra, who rises again each morning.
The sun disc between two hills: the horizon, where the sun sets and rises, between the lions of Yesterday and Tomorrow.
The running caption of Spell 17 above plate VII, with remnants of signs.
One of the two lions that hold up the horizon. In other copies this one is named Yesterday, which the spell explains as Osiris.
The sun boat sails with six gods standing in it, spears in hand. On a stand in the middle lies a crowned creature beneath the sun disc; what it is could not be identified.
A man holds up a lotus flower and a bunch of flowers before the sun boat.
A man raises both hands in praise before the sun boat.
A bird with a man's head and a god's beard stands on a low stand: the ba, the soul of the deceased, free to leave the tomb by day.
A falcon stands on a perch. The papyri give it no name.
The deceased sits in a booth before a senet board. The spell's title promises that he will play senet and sit in a booth in the afterlife.
The dead man stands with his staff, ready to set out. Spell 17 lets him come forth by day in any form he wishes.
